summary: This document specifies a TLS extension letting clients send generic user mapping hints in the supplemental data handshake message from RFC 4680. An informative section defines one hint, UpnDomainHint, which a server can use to find a user in a directory database. It updates RFC 4346 and was later updated by RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4681 lets a TLS client tell the server which account it thinks it is, without putting that information in the certificate. The client first offers a new extension in its hello. If the server accepts it, the client sends a short extra message before its certificate, saying for example that it wants to be treated as a user in a particular domain. The server can use that to find the right entry in a directory. The hint carries no proof of identity, so the server must still check the certificate itself.

subtitle: A TLS extension that lets a client hint which directory account its certificate belongs to.

tldr.problem: A certificate does not have to name the directory account it belongs to, so a server that wanted to map a client certificate to a user had no standard way to be told where to look.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds a TLS extension, user_mapping, that the client offers in its hello and the server accepts, and a new supplemental data message in which the client sends a list of mapping hints.
tldr.outcome: The server can use the hint to find the user's entry in a directory, then check the certificate against it. The hint itself is not trusted. RFC 4681 was later updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4681 was published in October 2006 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 8996. The extension is still the standard way for a TLS client to hint which directory account a certificate belongs to.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document has a normative part and an informative part. Sections 2 to 5 are normative, and section 6 is informative.

The specification defines a TLS extension and a payload for the SupplementalData handshake message, defined in RFC 4680, to accommodate mapping of users to their user accounts when using TLS client authentication as the authentication method.

The new TLS extension, user_mapping, is sent in the client hello message. Per the convention defined in RFC 4366, the server places the same extension in the server hello message to inform the client that the server understands it. If the server does not understand the extension, it responds with a server hello omitting it, and the client proceeds as normal, ignoring the extension and not including the UserMappingDataList data in the TLS handshake.

If the new extension is understood, the client injects UserMappingDataList data in the SupplementalData handshake message prior to the client's Certificate message. The server then parses this message, extracts the client's domain, and stores it in the context for use when mapping the certificate to the user's directory account. No other modifications to the protocol are required.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension is an offer and an answer. If the server says no, nothing changes and the handshake looks ordinary. If it says yes, one extra message appears before the client sends its certificate.

sections.title: Design Consideration
sections.content: The reason the mapping data itself is not placed in the extension portion of the client hello is to prevent broadcasting this information to servers that do not understand the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The client hello can be seen by any server it talks to. Putting the account name there would hand it out to servers that have no use for it, so it is sent separately and only after the server has agreed to receive it.

sections.title: The User Mapping Extension
sections.content:
A new extension type, user_mapping(6), is added to the Extension used in both the client hello and server hello messages. The extension_data field of this extension SHALL contain a UserMappingTypeList with a list of supported hint types, where the list is a vector of UserMappingType values of length 1 to 2^8-1.

The list of user_mapping_types included in a client hello SHALL signal the hint types supported by the client. The list included in the server hello SHALL signal the hint types preferred by the server. If none of the hint types listed by the client is supported by the server, the server SHALL omit the user_mapping extension in the server hello. When the user_mapping extension is included in the server hello, the list of hint types in the UserMappingTypeList SHALL be either equal to, or a subset of, the list provided by the client.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension carries a list of hint kinds the client understands. The server answers with the ones it prefers, which must be a subset of what the client offered, or it leaves the extension out entirely.

sections.title: The Supplemental Data Structures
sections.content:
The underlying structure of the SupplementalData handshake message, used to carry the information defined in this section, is defined in RFC 4680. A new SupplementalDataType is defined to accommodate communication of generic user mapping data.

The information in this data type carries one or more unauthenticated hints, a UserMappingDataList, inserted by the client side. Upon receipt and successful completion of the TLS handshake, the server MAY use this hint to locate the user's account from which user information and credentials MAY be retrieved to support authentication based on the client certificate.

The SupplementalDataEntry structure holds a supplemental data type, a 16-bit length, and a selection on the type whose only case is user_mapping_data carrying the UserMappingDataList. The user_mapping_data enumeration has the value 0.

The UserMappingData structure contains a user_mapping_version of type UserMappingType, a 16-bit user_mapping_length, and a selection on the type. The user_mapping_length field is the length in bytes of the data selected by UserMappingType. The UserMappingDataList is a vector of UserMappingData structures of length 1 to 2^16-1.

The UserMappingData structure contains a single mapping of type UserMappingType, and it can be leveraged to define new types of user mapping hints in the future. No preference is given to the order in which hints are specified in the vector. If the client sends more than one hint, the server SHOULD use the applicable mapping supported by the server. Implementations MAY support the UPN domain hint, and MAY also support other user mapping types as they are defined. Definitions of standards-track user mapping types must include a discussion of internationalization considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The message holds a list of hints. Each hint starts with a kind number and a length, then the data for that kind. More kinds can be added later without breaking this one.

sections.title: Message Flow
sections.content:
To negotiate sending user mapping data to a server in accordance with this specification, clients MUST include an extension of type user_mapping in the extended client hello, which SHALL contain a list of supported hint types.

Servers that receive an extended client hello containing a user_mapping extension MAY indicate that they are willing to accept user mapping data by including an extension of type user_mapping in the extended server hello, which SHALL contain a list of preferred hint types.

After negotiation of the use of user mapping has been successfully completed by exchanging hello messages including user_mapping extensions, clients MAY send a SupplementalData message containing the UserMappingDataList before the Certificate message.

The server MUST expect and gracefully handle the case where the client chooses not to send any supplementalData handshake message even after successful negotiation of extensions. The client MAY at its own discretion decide that the user mapping hint it initially intended to send is no longer relevant for this session. One such reason could be that the server certificate fails to meet certain requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The client offers, the server accepts, and the client then sends the hint before its certificate. The client is allowed to change its mind and send nothing at all, and the server has to cope with that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The user mapping hint sent in the UserMappingDataList is unauthenticated data that MUST NOT be treated as a trusted identifier. Authentication of the user represented by that user mapping hint MUST rely solely on validation of the client certificate. One way to do this is to use the user mapping hint to locate and extract a certificate of the claimed user from the trusted directory and subsequently match this certificate against the validated client certificate from the TLS handshake.

As the client is the initiator of this TLS extension, it needs to determine when it is appropriate to send the user mapping information. It may not be prudent to broadcast a user mapping hint to just any server at any time. To avoid superfluously sending user mapping hints, clients SHOULD only send this information if they recognize the server as a legitimate recipient. Recognition of the server can be done in many ways, for example by recognizing the name and address of the server.

In some cases the user mapping hint may itself be regarded as sensitive. In such cases, the double handshake technique described in RFC 4680 can be used to provide protection for the user mapping hint information.
sections.plainLanguage: The hint is a claim, not proof. The server must check the certificate against the directory entry the hint points at, and the client should only send the hint to a server it trusts.

sections.title: The UPN Domain Hint
sections.content:
This section gives an informative description of one user mapping hint type, for Domain Name hints and User Principal Name hints. Other hint types may be defined in other documents in the future.

The User Principal Name in this hint type represents a name that specifies a user's entry in a directory in the form userName@domainName. Traditionally, Microsoft has relied on the presence of such a name form in the client certificate when logging on to a domain account. However, this has several drawbacks, since it prevents the use of certificates with an absent UPN and also requires re-issuance of certificates, or issuance of multiple certificates, to reflect account changes or the creation of new accounts. The TLS extension, in combination with the defined hint type, provides a significant improvement to this situation, as it allows a single certificate to be mapped to one or more accounts of the user and does not require the certificate to contain a proprietary UPN.

The domain_name field MAY be used when only domain information is needed, for example where a user has accounts in multiple domains using the same user name, and where that user name is known from another source such as the client certificate. When the user name is also needed, the user_principal_name field MAY be used to indicate both user name and domain name. If both fields are present, the server can make use of whichever one it chooses.

The hint has the enumeration value upn_domain_hint(64) and carries an opaque user_principal_name of up to 2^16-1 bytes and an opaque domain_name of up to 2^16-1 bytes. The user_principal_name field, when specified, SHALL be of the form user@domain, where user is a UTF-8 encoded Unicode string that does not contain the @ character, and domain is a domain name. The domain_name field, when specified, SHALL contain a domain name in the usual text form, that is a sequence of one or more domain labels separated by dots, each domain label starting and ending with an alphanumeric character and possibly also containing hyphen characters. The field is an IDN-unaware domain name slot as defined in RFC 3490, so domain names containing non-ASCII characters have to be processed as described in RFC 3490 before being stored in it. The UpnDomainHint MUST at least contain a non-empty user_principal_name or a non-empty domain_name, and MAY contain both.
sections.plainLanguage: This hint carries the account name in two halves, so the server can be told just the domain when it already knows the user name. One certificate can then stand for several accounts.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has taken three actions. First, it created an entry, user_mapping(6), in the existing registry for ExtensionType defined in RFC 4366. Second, it created an entry, user_mapping_data(0), in the new registry for SupplementalDataType defined in RFC 4680. Third, it established a registry for TLS UserMappingType values, whose first entry is upn_domain_hint(64).

Values in the inclusive range 0 to 63 are assigned via RFC 2434 Standards Action. Values from the inclusive range 64 to 223 are assigned via RFC 2434 Specification Required. Values from the inclusive range 224 to 255 are reserved for RFC 2434 Private Use.
sections.plainLanguage: Three registry entries: the extension number, the supplemental data number, and a new range for hint kinds with a set of rules for who may assign them.
